contribution: Connecting an ammeter and a voltmeter is justified by the task of the meter and its own resistance; the multimeter's selector, jacks, measuring range and OL, the consequences of wrong connections (short circuit, interrupted current) and the manufacturer's error limit $\Delta x = p \cdot x + n \cdot r$ and, on its basis, the choice of the smallest suitable range.
learn: connect an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel and explain why.
choose the measuring range of a multimeter and calculate the error limit of a reading.
explain how the meter and a wrong connection affect the electric circuit.
prior: Electric current is a flow of charge through the cross-section of a conductor, and its unit is the ampere (chapter *Electric circuit, current and voltage*)
Voltage is a quantity between two points, and its unit is the volt (chapter *Electric circuit, current and voltage*)
A measurement result always has an uncertainty, and the resolution is the smallest step that the measuring instrument can show (chapter *Measuring and the reliability of a measurement*)

activities.text: On the physics lab bench there is a circuit in which a battery, a lamp and a resistor are one after another, and a multimeter with two test leads. The task sounds easy: measure the current and the voltage of the lamp. However, the places of the test leads and the position of the selector decide what the display tells: a wrongly connected meter can change how the circuit works.
activities.question: How are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected to a circuit, and why exactly in that way?

activities.title: Review: current and voltage
activities.prompt: Which of the following describes electric current and voltage correctly?

choices.text: Current is a flow of charge through the cross-section of a conductor, and voltage is a quantity between two points.
choices.feedback: Correct (chapter *Electric circuit, current and voltage*). That is why current is measured at a point through which the charge passes, and voltage between two points. This difference decides how the meters are connected.

choices.text: Current and voltage are two names for the same thing: both tell how much electricity there is in a wire.
choices.feedback: They are different quantities with different units, the ampere and the volt. Current tells how much charge passes through a cross-section in a second; voltage is a quantity between two points that is related to energy per charge.

choices.text: Voltage travels along the wire to the lamp, and current is produced only in the lamp.
choices.feedback: Voltage does not travel anywhere: it is always between two points, for example between the terminals of the battery or the terminals of the lamp. Current, on the other hand, flows at every point of a closed circuit, also in the wires.

choices.text: Current is a property of one point, and voltage tells how fast the charge moves.
choices.feedback: Current describes the passage of charge through a cross-section, and voltage is a quantity between two points. The speed of the charge carriers is neither of these.

activities.title: Prediction 1: current before and after the lamp
activities.prompt: In the circuit the battery, the lamp and the resistor are one after another without branches. An ammeter is connected in series first between the battery and the lamp, then between the lamp and the resistor. How do the readings differ?

choices.text: After the lamp the reading is smaller, because the lamp uses part of the current for light.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: both places give $97.8\,\text{mA}$. The lamp changes electrical energy into light and heat, but no charge disappears: as much charge comes out of the lamp as goes in.

choices.text: The readings are the same, because in a circuit without branches the same charge passes through all the components.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model support this: both places give $97.8\,\text{mA}$. Charge neither disappears nor accumulates, so the same amount of charge passes through every cross-section in a second. An ammeter can therefore be connected at any point of a circuit without branches.

choices.text: After the lamp the reading is larger, because the lamp accelerates the charge.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: both readings are $97.8\,\text{mA}$. The lamp does not add charge or current; it changes electrical energy into light and heat.

choices.text: Between the lamp and the resistor the current is zero, because the lamp has used it all up.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: also between the lamp and the resistor the current is $97.8\,\text{mA}$. If the current ended in the lamp, nothing would pass through the resistor, and the circuit would not be closed.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a voltmeter in series
activities.prompt: The voltage of the lamp is to be measured, but a voltmeter is connected in series by mistake: the circuit is opened between the battery and the lamp and the meter is placed in the gap. The voltage of the batteries is $4.5\,\text{V}$. Resistance describes how strongly the meter opposes the current: the resistance of a voltmeter is very large, for example $10\,\text{M}\Omega$, and that of an ammeter very small. What happens?

choices.text: The lamp is lit as before, and the meter shows the voltage of the lamp.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: in series the meter shows $4.50\,\text{V}$, and the lamp goes out. In parallel with the lamp the voltage of the lamp is only $1.50\,\text{V}$. The large resistance of the voltmeter stops the current when all the current has to pass through it.

choices.text: The lamp goes out, and the meter shows approximately the voltage of the battery.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model support this: in series the meter shows $4.50\,\text{V}$ and the lamp is not lit, in parallel with the lamp $1.50\,\text{V}$ while the lamp is lit. The resistance of the voltmeter is so large that the current decreases to almost zero, and almost the whole voltage of the battery is left between the terminals of the meter.

choices.text: The lamp is lit more brightly, because the meter adds voltage to the circuit.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: the lamp goes out. The meter is not a voltage source, and it does not add energy to the circuit; on the contrary, its large resistance stops the current.

choices.text: The fuse of the meter blows, because a large current passes through the meter.
choices.feedback: The readings of the model refute this: the fuse does not blow, and the meter shows $4.50\,\text{V}$. The large resistance of the voltmeter makes the current almost zero. A large current and a blown fuse belong to an ammeter that is wrongly connected in parallel.

activities.text: Choose the places of the test leads and the position of the selector. Follow the reading of the display and the lamp.
activities.howto: *Meter connection* chooses where the test leads are touched: in series into either gap of the upper wire, or in parallel with the lamp, the resistor or the battery. *Selector* chooses the quantity and the measuring range like the rotary switch of a real multimeter; on the current range $10\,\text{A}$ the red lead moves to its own jack. *Batteries* changes the number of batteries. The display shows the reading with the resolution of the range, or OL when the value is over the range. The purple arrows show the direction of the current from the positive terminal of the battery to the negative terminal when current flows in the circuit.
activities.model: The batteries are ideal: the voltage of each is $1.5\,\text{V}$ regardless of the current. The resistance of the lamp is constant $15\,\Omega$ in the model, although the resistance of a real filament lamp increases as it warms up, and the resistance of the resistor is $30\,\Omega$. The resistance of the meter itself is $10\,\text{M}\Omega$ on the voltage ranges, $1.0\,\Omega$ on the range $200\,\text{mA}$ and $0.010\,\Omega$ on the range $10\,\text{A}$. When a larger current than the range can show passes through the meter, the fuse blows and the meter is disconnected from the circuit; in the model a new fuse is in place as soon as the connection or the selector is changed. The readings are values calculated by the model, not measurements.
activities.calc: The model solves the current and the voltages of the circuit by means of the resistances, as in the chapter *Resistance and Ohm's law*, and the meter is in the circuit as one component with its own resistance. That is why on the range $200\,\text{mA}$ the current is $97.8\,\text{mA}$ and not $100\,\text{mA}$: the resistance of the meter itself decreases the current slightly, whereas on the range $10\,\text{A}$ the difference does not show. The reading of the display is rounded to the resolution of the range: $0.001\,\text{V}$, $0.01\,\text{V}$, $0.1\,\text{mA}$ or $0.01\,\text{A}$. In the model the lamp is lit when its power is at least $4\,\text{mW}$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the place of the ammeter
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The selector is on the range $200\,\text{mA}$ and there are three batteries. Change only the connection of the meter: record the reading at least in the places *in series before the lamp* and *in series between the lamp and the resistor*. Finally also try *in parallel with the lamp*: what happens to the lamp, what does the meter show and what happens to the meter?

kytkenta.sarja2: in series between the lamp and the resistor

activities.title: Experiment 2: a voltmeter in parallel and in series
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The selector is on the range $20\,\text{V}$ and there are three batteries. Change only the connection of the meter: record the reading at least in the places *in parallel with the lamp* and *in series before the lamp*, preferably also *in parallel with the battery*. In which connection is the lamp lit, and what voltage does the meter show in each?

kytkenta.sarja2: in series between the lamp and the resistor

activities.title: Experiment 3: measuring range
activities.intro: The meter is in parallel with the lamp, and there are three batteries. Change only the position of the selector: record the reading on the ranges $20\,\text{V}$ and $2\,\text{V}$. How many decimals does the display show on each range? Then move the meter in parallel with the resistor on the range $2\,\text{V}$: what does the display tell, and what must be done then?

kytkenta.sarja2: in series between the lamp and the resistor

activities.title: Conclusion: how the meters are connected
activities.prompt: Write on the basis of your tables: how did the reading of the ammeter depend on its place in a circuit without branches? What happened when the voltmeter was in parallel with the lamp, and what when it was in series? Explain the observations with the resistances of the meters.
activities.model: The ammeter showed $97.8\,\text{mA}$ both before the lamp and between the lamp and the resistor: in a circuit without branches the same charge passes through every component, so the current is the same at every point. In parallel with the lamp the voltmeter showed $1.50\,\text{V}$, and the lamp was lit, because hardly any current passes through the large resistance of the meter past the lamp. Connected in series, the same meter showed $4.50\,\text{V}$, and the lamp went out: the large resistance of the meter decreased the current of the whole circuit to almost zero, and almost the whole voltage of the battery was left between the terminals of the meter. If the ammeter was connected in parallel with the lamp, the lamp went out, because the current passed through the meter of small resistance past the lamp. That is why an ammeter is connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel. The values are calculated by the model.
criteria: I said that the reading of the ammeter was the same in both series places, and explained it by the fact that charge does not disappear.
I gave the readings of the voltmeter in parallel ($1.50\,\text{V}$, the lamp is lit) and in series ($4.50\,\text{V}$, the lamp goes out).
I explained that the large resistance of the voltmeter stops the current in series and the small resistance of the ammeter bypasses the lamp in parallel.
I stated that the readings are values of the model.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the readings of the experiments. Then return to the question at the beginning: why are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected to a circuit in different ways?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
A student measures the reading $6.00\,\text{V}$ on the range $20\,\text{V}$. The error limit is $\pm(0.5\,\% + 2\ \text{digits})$. The student calculates

$$\begin{aligned} &\Delta U \\ &= 0.005 \cdot 6.00\,\text{V} + 2\,\text{V} \\ &= 2.03\,\text{V} \end{aligned}$$

Where is the error?

choices.text: Two digits means two steps of the last digit, that is $2 \cdot 0.01\,\text{V}$, so $\Delta U = 0.050\,\text{V}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. On the range $20\,\text{V}$ the last digit is a hundredth of a volt, so the share of the digits is $0.02\,\text{V}$ and not $2\,\text{V}$. The result could have been seen to be wrong at once: an error limit of $2.03\,\text{V}$ would be a third of the whole reading.

choices.text: The percentage is wrong: $0.5\,\%$ as a decimal number is $0.5$, so $\Delta U = 5.0\,\text{V}$.
choices.feedback: Percent means a hundredth, so $0.5\,\% = 0.005$, and the student has written it correctly. The error is in the share of the digits: two digits is $2 \cdot 0.01\,\text{V}$.

choices.text: The percentage part and the digits should be multiplied together, not added.
choices.feedback: The error limit is the sum of two parts: the percentage of the reading plus the share of the digits. The error is in the share of the digits: one digit is the resolution of the range $0.01\,\text{V}$, not $1\,\text{V}$.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation: on the range $20\,\text{V}$ the meter is inaccurate, so a large error limit is correct.
choices.feedback: With this reading the error limit is less than a percent of the reading ($0.050\,\text{V} : 6.00\,\text{V} \approx 0.8\,\%$). In the calculation one digit has been interpreted as one volt, although it is the resolution of the range $0.01\,\text{V}$.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: The current of an LED is first measured on the range $10\,\text{A}$ of a multimeter, because a friend says it is the safest. The display shows $0.02\,\text{A}$. The resolution of the range is $0.01\,\text{A}$ and the error limit $\pm(2.0\,\% + 3\ \text{digits})$. What percentage of the reading is the error limit?
hints: The error limit consists of the percentage part and the share of the digits. Which of them is larger here?
One digit is the resolution of the range $0.01\,\text{A}$, so three digits is $0.03\,\text{A}$. The percentage part is $0.020 \cdot 0.02\,\text{A}$.
$\Delta I = 0.0004\,\text{A} + 0.03\,\text{A} = 0.0304\,\text{A}$; divide this by the reading $0.02\,\text{A}$.

mistakes.feedback: You took into account only the percentage part. The share of the digits $3 \cdot 0.01\,\text{A} = 0.03\,\text{A}$ is here much larger than the whole reading, and that is exactly what makes measuring a small current on a large range inaccurate.
You used $0.001\,\text{A}$ as the step of a digit. On the range $10\,\text{A}$ the display has two decimals, so one digit is $0.01\,\text{A}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** reading $I = 0.02\,\text{A}$ on the range $10\,\text{A}$, resolution $r = 0.01\,\text{A}$, error limit $\pm(2.0\,\% + 3\ \text{digits})$

**Find:** the relative error limit $\tfrac{\Delta I}{I}$ as a percentage

**Principle:** The manufacturer's error limit is a percentage of the reading plus three steps of the last digit. When the reading is very small compared with the range, the share of the digits does not decrease with the reading, so it dominates the error limit.

**Formula:** $\Delta I = p \cdot I + n \cdot r$, so

$$\frac{\Delta I}{I} = \frac{p \cdot I + n \cdot r}{I}$$

**Conversions:** $p = 2.0\,\% = 0.020$; the currents are in amperes.

**Substitution:** $\Delta I = 0.020 \cdot 0.02\,\text{A} + 3 \cdot 0.01\,\text{A} = 0.0004\,\text{A} + 0.03\,\text{A} = 0.0304\,\text{A}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta I}{I} = \dfrac{0.0304\,\text{A}}{0.02\,\text{A}} = 1.52 = 152\,\%$

**Answer:** about $150\,\%$; the reading $0.02\,\text{A}$ is given with one significant figure, so the result is only an order of magnitude.

**Reasonableness:** Already three steps, $0.03\,\text{A}$, are larger than the whole reading, so the error limit must be over $100\,\%$. The reading therefore tells almost nothing about the current. On the range $200\,\text{mA}$ the same current could appear for example as $18.6\,\text{mA}$, and the error limit would be $0.186\,\text{mA} + 0.2\,\text{mA} = 0.386\,\text{mA}$, or about $2\,\%$: when the order of magnitude is known, one moves to the smallest suitable range.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. In the tasks of level 1 an error limit is calculated or one observation is used, in the tasks of level 2 two steps are combined, such as a conversion and the error limit, and level 3 requires reasoning in a new situation.

activities.title: 1. Connecting an ammeter
activities.prompt: We want to measure how large a current passes through the resistor in a circuit in which a battery, a lamp and a resistor are one after another. How is the ammeter connected?

choices.text: The circuit is opened next to the resistor, and the meter is placed in the gap, so the current of the resistor passes through the meter.
choices.feedback: Correct. An ammeter measures the current passing through it, so it is connected in series. In a circuit without branches the gap can be made at any point, because the current is the same at every point.

choices.text: The leads of the meter are touched to both ends of the resistor without opening the circuit.
choices.feedback: This is how a voltmeter is connected. An ammeter in parallel with the resistor makes a short circuit: the current passes through the meter of small resistance past the resistor, and the fuse of the meter may blow.

choices.text: One lead of the meter is touched to the positive terminal of the battery and the other to the negative terminal.
choices.feedback: An ammeter between the terminals of the battery is a short circuit for the whole battery: the current becomes very large, and the fuse of the meter blows. The voltage of the battery is measured between the terminals with a voltmeter.

choices.text: The meter is connected in series, but only after the resistor, because before the resistor the current is larger.
choices.feedback: In a circuit without branches the current is the same at every point: the resistor does not use up current, so the meter shows the same reading before and after the resistor.

activities.title: 2. Error limit of a reading
activities.prompt: The voltage of a lamp is measured on the range $2\,\text{V}$, and the display shows $0.846\,\text{V}$. The resolution of the range is $0.001\,\text{V}$ and the error limit $\pm(0.5\,\% + 2\ \text{digits})$. How large is the error limit of the reading? Give the answer in millivolts.
hints: The error limit is a percentage of the reading plus two steps of the last digit.
The percentage part is $0.005 \cdot 0.846\,\text{V}$ and the share of the digits $2 \cdot 0.001\,\text{V}$.
$\Delta U = 0.00423\,\text{V} + 0.002\,\text{V}$; convert the result to millivolts by multiplying by a thousand.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated only the percentage part. Add to it two steps of the last digit, $2 \cdot 0.001\,\text{V} = 2\,\text{mV}$.
You used the resolution $0.01\,\text{V}$ of the range $20\,\text{V}$. On the range $2\,\text{V}$ the display has three decimals, so one digit is $0.001\,\text{V}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** reading $U = 0.846\,\text{V}$ on the range $2\,\text{V}$, resolution $r = 0.001\,\text{V}$, error limit $\pm(0.5\,\% + 2\ \text{digits})$

**Find:** the error limit $\Delta U$ in millivolts

**Principle:** The manufacturer's error limit is a share of the reading plus two steps of the last digit. One digit is the resolution of the range, here $0.001\,\text{V}$.

**Formula:** $\Delta U = p \cdot U + n \cdot r$

**Conversions:** $p = 0.5\,\% = 0.005$; finally $1\,\text{V} = 1000\,\text{mV}$.

**Substitution:** $\Delta U = 0.005 \cdot 0.846\,\text{V} + 2 \cdot 0.001\,\text{V} = 0.00423\,\text{V} + 0.002\,\text{V} = 0.00623\,\text{V} = 0.00623 \cdot 1000\,\text{mV} = 6.23\,\text{mV}$

**Answer:** $6.2\,\text{mV}$, two significant figures, because the error limit is an estimate.

**Reasonableness:** Half a percent of a little less than a volt is a little over $4\,\text{mV}$, and two steps add $2\,\text{mV}$. The relative error limit is less than a percent, as it should be on the smallest suitable range.

activities.title: 3. Explain: the resistance of the meter itself
activities.prompt: Why must the resistance of a good voltmeter be very large and that of a good ammeter very small? Explain for each what happens in the meter and in the circuit when the meter is connected correctly.
criteria: I explained that the voltmeter is in parallel with the component, so the current through it bypasses the component and changes the circuit; a large resistance keeps this current very small.
I explained that the ammeter is in series, so the whole current passes through it; a small resistance keeps the voltage left across the meter and the change in the current small.
I stated that a real meter always changes the circuit a little, which is one source of measurement uncertainty.
activities.model: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component, so a parallel path past the component forms through it. If the resistance of the meter were small, part of the current would pass through the meter, the current and the voltage of the component would change, and the meter would show a different value than without the meter. A large resistance, for example $10\,\text{M}\Omega$, keeps the current of the meter so small that the circuit practically does not change. An ammeter, on the other hand, is connected in series, so the whole current to be measured passes through it. If its resistance were large, it would decrease exactly the current that is being measured, and part of the voltage of the battery would be left across the meter. A small resistance keeps this effect small: in the simulation the meter of the range $200\,\text{mA}$ decreased the current by only about $2\,\%$. An ideal meter would not change the circuit at all, but a real meter always changes it a little, which is one source of measurement uncertainty.

activities.text: Finally two quick questions. Answer first yourself and open the answer only then.
